scenes.text: Have you noticed that AI sometimes makes things up, and says them with total confidence? [1] And why does the same question give you a different answer every time? [2] In this episode, let's understand temperature, and hallucinations.

Remember, an LLM picks the next word from a list of likely options. [1] Temperature controls how adventurous that pick is. [2] With a low temperature, it plays it safe, [3] and with a high temperature, it takes more risks. [4] So it's the same model, just with a different personality.

data.definition: A setting that controls how random or creative the AI's word choices are.

scenes.text: Let's turn the dial and see. Our prompt is, describe the moon in one line. [1] At zero, you get a plain, factual answer, and it's the same every single time. [2] Around point seven, it becomes more vivid and interesting. [3] And at one, it gets wild and poetic, and sometimes, a little too wild.

data.heading: Turn the dial
data.prompt: Describe the Moon in one line.
settings: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.
The Moon is a silver lantern hanging over a quiet sea.
The Moon: a cosmic cheese-wheel humming lullabies to sleepy comets.

scenes.text: So when should you use which? [1] Here's a quick cheat sheet. [2] For maths and facts, keep the temperature low. [3] For writing code, keep it low as well. [4] For brainstorming ideas, turn it up, [5] and for poems and stories, go high.

Now, let's talk about hallucinations. [1] A hallucination is when the AI confidently says something that isn't true. It could be [2] made up facts, [3] made up quotes, [4] or even citations to research papers that don't exist at all.

data.definition: When the AI confidently makes up something that isn't true.

scenes.text: So why does this happen? [1] Well, the model is trained to sound fluent, not to check facts. [2] So when it doesn't know something, it still predicts an answer that sounds right. [3] And a higher temperature adds more randomness, which means more risk.

So how do you protect yourself? [1] Ask for sources, and actually open and check them. [2] Give it the facts yourself, right inside the prompt, and that's the idea behind RAG, which is coming up soon. [3] And tell it clearly, if you're not sure, just say I don't know.

data.heading: How to reduce it
items: Make it OK to be unsure
